seo.title: Technologies
seo.description: The stack Altrazen builds on: TypeScript, React, Next.js, React Native, Node, PostgreSQL and the tooling around them — and why each one is there.

hero.heading: What we build with, and why
hero.description: A short list we know deeply, rather than a long one we have touched once. Everything here is in production on work we maintain.

intro.heading: Boring technology, chosen deliberately
paragraphs: Every tool on this page earns its place by being well understood, widely supported and unlikely to be abandoned. That is not conservatism for its own sake — it is what makes a codebase possible to hand to someone else, hire for, and still run in five years.

We do not add a technology to your stack because we wanted to learn it. If something here is wrong for your problem we will say so, and if the right answer is a tool we do not use, we will tell you that instead of taking the work.

categories.label: Language
categories.description: One language across the stack, so the same people can work at both ends of a feature.

items.name: TypeScript
items.note: Strict mode everywhere. Types are the cheapest documentation there is, and the only kind that cannot go stale.

items.name: SQL
items.note: Written directly when a query matters. An ORM is a convenience, not a reason to stop understanding the query plan.

categories.label: Front end
categories.description: Interfaces that stay fast on a mid-range phone, not just on a developer's laptop.

items.name: React
items.note: Server components by default; client components only where there is genuine interactivity to justify the JavaScript.

items.name: Next.js
items.note: Static generation wherever the content allows it. This site is a static export with no server behind it.

items.name: Tailwind CSS
items.note: Design tokens defined once and used everywhere, so a colour or spacing value cannot drift across a codebase.

categories.label: Mobile
categories.description: One codebase for both platforms, dropping to native only where a capability requires it.

items.name: React Native
items.note: Shared logic with the web where it makes sense, and native modules where a platform capability genuinely needs them.

items.name: Expo
items.note: Build pipeline, over-the-air updates and store submission without maintaining custom build infrastructure.

categories.label: Back end and data
categories.description: The part that decides whether an application is still fast at ten thousand users.

items.name: Node.js
items.note: The same language and types as the front end, which removes a whole category of contract bugs between them.

items.name: PostgreSQL
items.note: The default unless there is a specific reason otherwise. Correct indexes solve more performance problems than a bigger instance.

items.name: Redis
items.note: Caching, rate limiting and job queues. Added when there is a measured need, not by default.

categories.label: Infrastructure
categories.description: Deployments that can be reversed, on accounts you own.

items.name: Docker
items.note: Reproducible environments, so "works on my machine" stops being a category of bug.

items.name: Vercel
items.note: For static and edge-rendered front ends, with preview deployments on every pull request.

items.name: AWS
items.note: Where an application needs more than a front-end host. Infrastructure defined as code rather than clicked together in a console.

items.name: GitHub Actions
items.note: Tests, type checks, accessibility and performance budgets run on every pull request and block the merge if they fail.

categories.label: Quality and operations
categories.description: The tooling that turns a silent failure into a message someone reads.

items.name: Playwright
items.note: End-to-end coverage on the paths where a failure costs money: payment, authentication, data writes.

items.name: Vitest
items.note: Unit and integration tests. We write tests where they earn their keep, not to reach a coverage number.

items.name: Error tracking
items.note: Structured errors routed to a person. An error nobody is told about is the same as no error handling at all.

principles.heading: Four rules for adding anything to a stack

items.title: It has to be hireable
items.description: If your next developer cannot be found or cannot pick it up in a week, it is a liability regardless of how good it is.

items.title: It has to be reversible
items.description: We prefer tools you can migrate away from. Anything that would take a rewrite to leave gets a written decision record explaining why we accepted that.

items.title: It has to earn the dependency
items.description: Every package is code you now maintain and a vulnerability you may inherit. The standard library and a few lines of your own often win.

items.title: It has to be observable
items.description: If we cannot see what it is doing in production, we cannot support it, and neither can you.

cta.heading: Not sure this fits your problem?
cta.description: Tell us what you are building. If the right answer is outside what we do, we will say so on the first call.
